title: Selected Work
text:
SELECTED WORK



Much of my recent consulting work involved proprietary client data, internal code, or private decision-support products, so it cannot be posted publicly. The examples below focus on the problem solved, my role, and the capabilities demonstrated without exposing confidential assets.

title: Selected Work
text:
Reusable client dashboard framework
Problem. Recurring client deliverables depended heavily on static reports and slide decks. One-off production made it difficult to maintain consistency, reduce revision cycles, reuse components, and give decision-makers access to the deeper data behind top-level findings.
My role. Led development of reusable dashboard components and analytic workflows for health workforce projection and reporting projects.
Approach. Standardized recurring analyses and data preparation, developed modular R/Shiny components, strengthened validation workflows, and supported deployment through Posit Connect. The framework preserved client-specific flexibility while making the underlying process more repeatable.
Tools and methods. R · Shiny · Posit Connect · SQL · Excel · reproducible reporting · data validation
Demonstrates. Dashboard and application development, client-facing analytics, reusable data-product design, workflow modernization, and communication across technical and non-technical stakeholders.

title: Selected Work
text:
Workforce projection modeling
Problem. State agencies, hospital associations, professional societies, and other organizations needed defensible estimates of future workforce supply and demand for planning, education, policy, advocacy, and investment decisions.
My role. Managed economists and contributed directly to analytic design, projection methods, data processing, validation, reporting, stakeholder communication, and final deliverables.
Approach. Integrated licensing, education, demographic, survey, utilization, and labor-market data into reproducible workflows. Built and reviewed projections, tested outputs, translated assumptions and uncertainty for non-technical audiences, and produced public-facing reports and presentations.
Tools and methods. R · SQL · Excel · survey and administrative data · geospatial analysis · projection modeling · reproducible reporting
Demonstrates. Statistical modeling, data integration, applied research, executive communication, and end-to-end analytic delivery.

title: Selected Work
section: Data workflow modernization and architecture evaluation
text:
Data workflow modernization and architecture evaluation
Problem. Analytic teams can inherit fragmented files, repeated manual processes, undocumented dependencies, and infrastructure proposals that are more complex or expensive than their actual needs.
My role. Evaluated practical approaches to storing, querying, validating, documenting, and reusing recurring analytic datasets.
Approach. Developed proof-of-concept workflows using lightweight, analyst-friendly tools and compared alternatives based on performance, cost, maintainability, team skill, and handoff risk. One example used DuckDB with object-storage-oriented workflows as a simpler direct-query architecture for analytic workloads.
Tools and methods. DuckDB · object storage · R · SQL · dataset profiling · validation checks · documentation · reproducible pipelines
Demonstrates. Data architecture, pragmatic engineering judgment, cost-aware technical decision-making, and process modernization.

title: Selected Work
section: Public survey modernization and data collection strategy
text:
Public survey modernization and data collection strategy
Problem. Workforce data programs needed more complete, timely, and policy-relevant information without creating a data collection process disconnected from existing institutional workflows.
My role. Led survey design, data collection strategy, data linkage, analysis, and recurring reporting for health workforce supply and demand studies.
Approach. Improved survey instruments, aligned collection with licensing and renewal processes, linked survey and administrative data where appropriate, and converted recurring analysis into more repeatable workflows.
Tools and methods. Survey design · R · SQL · administrative data · licensing data · data linkage · reporting automation
Demonstrates. Research design, stakeholder needs assessment, data governance awareness, operational analytics, and system design under real-world constraints.

title: About
text:
ABOUT



I am a data and analytics consultant with more than 15 years of experience building analytic products, workforce models, research programs, dashboards, and decision-support systems for government, healthcare, associations, nonprofits, and consulting clients.
The recurring theme in my work is translating an ambiguous organizational problem into something concrete: a research question, a data strategy, a model, a dashboard, a workflow, or a system that people can actually use.
View my resume Contact me

title: About
text:
Background
Most recently I served as Director of Health Workforce Consulting at GlobalData, leading complex analytics engagements for state agencies, hospital associations, professional societies, and federal clients. My work included workforce projection methods, reusable R/Shiny dashboard frameworks, validation and documentation systems, and a DuckDB + object-storage proof of concept for lower-friction analytic architecture.
Before that, I helped establish Utah’s legislatively created Health Workforce Information Center and spent more than a decade at the Utah Medical Education Council, where I led statewide research programs covering multiple health professions and built survey, modeling, reporting, data-integration, cloud-hosted analytics, and public R/Shiny capabilities.
Earlier public-sector and nonprofit work gave me practical experience with programs, policy, operations, grants, administrative systems, and direct service. That experience still shapes how I approach analytics: the data system is never separate from the people, workflows, institutions, and decisions around it.

title: About
text:
How I think about consulting


Understand the decision before designing the analysis
A technically elegant answer to the wrong question is still the wrong answer.


Stakeholder input is part of system design
Usability, trust, incentives, workflow, and implementation constraints should shape the solution from the beginning.


Prefer maintainable over impressive
The right architecture is the one the organization can understand, afford, validate, and sustain.


Analysis is not finished when the model runs
Interpretation, communication, implementation, documentation, and handoff are part of the analytic product.

title: About
text:
Education and perspective
I hold four degrees from the University of Utah: an MBA with a Certificate in Information Systems, an MPA focused on Program Evaluation and Policy Analysis, a B.A. in Political Science with a Certificate in International Relations, and a B.A. in Spanish.
My professional work has crossed public policy, healthcare, labor and workforce analysis, program evaluation, data science, analytics engineering, and technical product delivery. I have also served as a peer reviewer, federal grant reviewer, nursing workforce center board president, and Salt Lake City planning commissioner and commission chair.
One project that strongly influenced how I think about analytics implementation was an IBM Health Corps collaboration focused on modeling primary-care workforce needs. The technical analysis mattered, but so did stakeholder participation, system design, usability, and the practical question of how a new analytic approach would be deployed and used.

section: The tool comes after the problem.
text:
The tool comes after the problem.


01 · Start with the decision
Define what someone needs to know, decide, or change before deciding what to build.


02 · Design with stakeholders
Understand how people work, what they trust, and what will make a solution usable in practice.


03 · Build for repeatability
Prefer transparent, documented workflows that can be validated, updated, and handed off.


04 · Make implementation part of the work
A technically correct solution that never gets adopted is not a successful analytics project.
